Epinephrine (adrenaline) is an animal hormone that stimulates the breakdown of the storage polysaccharide glycogen within liver cells and skeletal muscle cells to release glucose. The liver or muscle cell can use this compound for energy production (cellular respiration) or release glucose into the bloodstream. The overall effect of epinephrine is the mobilization of fuel reserves in situations in which the animals need to either defend themselves (fight) or escape whatever elicited a scare (flight).

Epinephrine stimulates glycogen breakdown by activating a cytosolic enzyme, glycogen phosphorylase. However, epinephrine does not interact directly with the enzyme responsible for glycogen breakdown; a series of intermediate steps must occur inside the cell.

First, the epinephrine binds to a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) in liver cells. An enzyme embedded in the plasma membrane, adenylyl cyclase, will be activated and then convert ATP to cyclic AMP (or cAMP), a second messenger. The cAMP broadcasts the signal to the cytoplasm. This molecule does not persist for long in the absence of the hormone because another enzyme, called phosphodiesterase, converts cAMP to AMP.
